title: What are Flink state backends — HashMapStateBackend (in-memory, fast, limited by JVM heap) vs EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend (on-disk, handles very large state, slower per-access) — and how do you choose (state size vs latency requirements)?

s1_definition.profdef: A Flink state backend determines where and how an operator's working state is stored while a job runs and how it is organized for checkpointing. The HashMapStateBackend keeps all state as regular Java objects on the JVM heap, giving the fastest possible per-access latency but bounding total state to available heap memory and exposing it to garbage-collection pressure. The EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend stores state in an embedded RocksDB instance on local disk as serialized bytes, which supports state far larger than memory and enables incremental checkpoints, at the cost of serialization and disk access on every state operation. The choice is a direct tradeoff between how much state you hold and how low your per-access latency must be.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's clerk keeping customer passbooks either on the desk or in a filing cabinet. The HashMapStateBackend is like keeping every passbook open on the desk: reaching any passbook is instant, but the desk only has room for a limited number before it overflows. The EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend is like keeping the passbooks in a well-indexed filing cabinet: there is effectively unlimited room for millions of passbooks, but each lookup costs a few extra seconds to pull the right drawer and read it. For a small branch with a handful of accounts you keep everything on the desk for speed; for a national system with hundreds of millions of accounts you must use the filing cabinet.
s1_definition.oneliner: HashMapStateBackend is heap-fast but memory-bounded, while RocksDB is disk-backed and huge but slower per access, so pick by state size versus latency needs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Flink state backend determines where and how an operator's working state is stored while a job runs and how it is organized for checkpointing. The HashMapStateBackend keeps all state as regular Java objects on the JVM heap, giving the fastest possible per-access latency but bounding total state to available heap memory and exposing it to garbage-collection pressure. The EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend stores state in an embedded RocksDB instance on local disk as serialized bytes, which supports state far larger than memory and enables incremental checkpoints, at the cost of serialization and disk access on every state operation. The choice is a direct tradeoff between how much state you hold and how low your per-access latency must be.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India's clerk keeping customer passbooks either on the desk or in a filing cabinet. The HashMapStateBackend is like keeping every passbook open on the desk: reaching any passbook is instant, but the desk only has room for a limited number before it overflows. The EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend is like keeping the passbooks in a well-indexed filing cabinet: there is effectively unlimited room for millions of passbooks, but each lookup costs a few extra seconds to pull the right drawer and read it. For a small branch with a handful of accounts you keep everything on the desk for speed; for a national system with hundreds of millions of accounts you must use the filing cabinet.

**One line to remember:** HashMapStateBackend is heap-fast but memory-bounded, while RocksDB is disk-backed and huge but slower per access, so pick by state size versus latency needs.

sections.s2_technical:
The HashMapStateBackend holds state as live Java objects in a hash map on the task manager heap. Because state is plain objects, reads and writes are extremely fast with no serialization, which gives the lowest per-access latency. The downsides are that total state is limited by the heap you can give the JVM, large heaps cause longer and more disruptive garbage-collection pauses, and a checkpoint of this backend is a full snapshot of all the objects, serialized and sent to durable storage, which means checkpoint cost grows with total state. This backend is ideal when the entire keyed state comfortably fits in memory, for example tens of gigabytes or less, and you need the absolute lowest latency.

The EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend stores state in an embedded RocksDB database, a log-structured key-value store, on the local disk of each task manager, keeping state as serialized bytes. Every state access must serialize the key, look it up in RocksDB, and deserialize the value, which adds latency compared to heap objects, but it means the working state can be much larger than memory, scaling to hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes per task manager because it spills to disk. Critically, RocksDB supports incremental checkpoints: instead of snapshotting all state each time, Flink uploads only the RocksDB files that changed since the last checkpoint, so checkpoint cost scales with the delta rather than the full state, which is essential for very large state. It also keeps most state off the JVM heap, avoiding garbage-collection pressure.

How you choose comes down to two questions: how big is your state, and how tight is your latency budget. If your state fits comfortably in heap and you need minimal latency, use HashMapStateBackend. If your state is large, grows over time, or must survive without ballooning the heap and garbage collection, use RocksDB and accept the per-access overhead, which is often negligible relative to network and sink latency. The senior nuances are several. RocksDB benefits enormously from fast local SSDs and from tuning its block cache and write buffers. RocksDB enables incremental checkpoints, which is often the deciding factor for jobs with many gigabytes of state, because full snapshots would otherwise dominate runtime. You should also size things with headroom, because RocksDB uses off-heap native memory that must be budgeted alongside the JVM. In practice, most large production Flink jobs at a bank, where per-account state across hundreds of millions of accounts is huge and must be durable, run on RocksDB, while small, latency-critical jobs with modest state run on HashMap.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a small, latency-critical job that tracks the running count of failed login attempts for the few thousand internal admin accounts, and it must react in microseconds because it gates access to sensitive systems. This state is tiny and the latency requirement is extreme, so keeping it as plain objects on the heap is ideal. This is exactly the HashMapStateBackend case: small state, lowest latency.

Problem 2 — The same bank runs a huge job that maintains a rolling ninety-day transaction history per account across hundreds of millions of retail accounts for fraud scoring. That state is far too large to fit in heap, grows continuously, and must be checkpointed efficiently without snapshotting everything each time. This is exactly the EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend case: very large state, disk-backed, incremental checkpoints, latency secondary.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that abstracts a state backend behind an interface and provides both implementations so you can see the behavioral difference. We define a `StateBackend` interface with put, get, and a checkpoint that reports its cost. A `HeapStateBackend` stores plain objects in a map, offers instant access, but reports a full-snapshot checkpoint cost proportional to total entries. A `RocksDbStateBackend` simulates serialization overhead per access and reports an incremental checkpoint cost proportional only to the number of changed entries since the last checkpoint. A `StateBackendDemo` main class runs the same workload through both, printing access behavior and the dramatically different checkpoint costs, illustrating why large state favors RocksDB.

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  backend:
    type: rocksdb              # heap | rocksdb
    rocksdb:
      local-dir: /mnt/ssd/flink/rocksdb
      incremental-checkpoints: true
      block-cache-mb: 512
    heap:
      max-heap-gb: 16
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a workload that seeds one thousand accounts, takes a checkpoint, then changes only three accounts and takes a second checkpoint, run through both the heap backend and the RocksDB backend.

Step 1, Heap backend: One thousand accounts are put as plain Java objects into the heap map, each write instant with no serialization. A first checkpoint runs, and because the heap backend takes a full snapshot, its cost is proportional to all one thousand entries.

Step 2, Heap continues: Three accounts change, Rajesh to 800, Priya to 800, and one other to 999, each write instant. The second checkpoint again takes a full snapshot, so its cost is still proportional to all one thousand entries, even though only three changed. This is the heap backend's weakness at scale: checkpoint cost does not shrink when few things change.

Step 3, Heap read: Reading Rajesh's balance returns 800 instantly as a direct object lookup, demonstrating the heap backend's lowest-latency access.

Step 4, RocksDB backend: One thousand accounts are put, but each value is serialized to bytes and stored in the disk-backed store, and each changed key is marked dirty. The first checkpoint is incremental, uploading the one thousand changed entries since there was nothing before.

Step 5, RocksDB continues: The same three accounts change. Each write serializes to bytes and marks exactly those three keys dirty. The second checkpoint is incremental and uploads only the three changed entries, so its cost is three rather than one thousand, even though a thousand accounts remain on disk. This is the decisive advantage for large state.

Step 6, RocksDB read: Reading Rajesh's balance deserializes the bytes back into a BigDecimal, which is correct at 800 but carries a small serialization cost compared to the heap backend. The demo makes the contrast concrete: heap is faster per access but pays a full-snapshot checkpoint, while RocksDB pays per-access serialization but checkpoints incrementally, which is why huge state lives on RocksDB.

```
  Keyed state operations (put/get per account)
    │
    ├────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
    ▼                            ▼                            │
  HashMapStateBackend          EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend    │
  heap: live Java objects      disk: serialized bytes         │
    │ put/get = instant          │ put/get = serialize/deser   │
    │ bounded by heap            │ scales past memory (SSD)    │
    ▼                            ▼                             │
  checkpoint = FULL snapshot   checkpoint = INCREMENTAL        │
  cost ~ total entries         cost ~ CHANGED entries          │
    │                            │                             │
    └──────────────┬─────────────┘                             │
                   ▼                                           ▼
          durable store (S3/HDFS)                 CHOOSE:
          heap second ckpt cost=1000               small+low latency → heap
          rocksdb second ckpt cost=3               large+durable     → rocksdb
```

  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ HeapStateBackend │  │ RocksDbStateBackend       │
  │ - heap: Map      │  │ - disk: Map<String,byte[]>│
  │ FULL snapshot    │  │ - dirtySinceCheckpoint:Set│
  │ instant access   │  │ INCREMENTAL, serialize    │
  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── Decision Diagram: Which Backend? ──────────────────────────

  [STATE PROFILE]
     │
     ├─ fits in heap AND latency critical ──→ HashMapStateBackend
     │
     ├─ large/growing OR must avoid GC ─────→ EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend
     │
     └─ many GB state + frequent checkpoints → RocksDB (incremental wins)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ────────────────────────────────

  1. rocksdb.put("ACC0".."ACC999") → 1000 dirty keys
  2. rocksdb.checkpoint() → upload 1000, clear dirty
  3. rocksdb.put(SAV2001/CUR3001/ACC42) → 3 dirty keys
  4. rocksdb.checkpoint() → upload ONLY 3 (incremental)
  5. heap.checkpoint() same step → upload ALL 1000 (full)

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Flink state backend decides where your operator's working state lives while the job runs and how it is organized for checkpointing, and the two main choices are the HashMapStateBackend and the EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend. The HashMapStateBackend keeps all state as regular Java objects on the task manager heap, which means reads and writes are extremely fast because there is no serialization, giving you the lowest per-access latency. Its limits are that total state is bounded by the heap you can afford, large heaps cause longer garbage-collection pauses, and its checkpoints are full snapshots whose cost grows with the entire state size. It is the right choice when the whole keyed state comfortably fits in memory and you need minimal latency.

The EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend stores state as serialized bytes in an embedded RocksDB key-value store on local disk. Every access serializes the key, looks it up, and deserializes the value, which adds latency, but in return the working state can be far larger than memory, scaling to hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes by spilling to disk, and most of it stays off the JVM heap so garbage collection is not a problem. The decisive advantage for large jobs is incremental checkpoints: instead of snapshotting everything, Flink uploads only the RocksDB files that changed since the last checkpoint, so checkpoint cost tracks the delta rather than the total. You pick it when state is large, growing, or must be durable without ballooning the heap, and you give it fast local SSDs and budget its off-heap native memory.

At the National Bank of India we ran both, deliberately, on different jobs. A small, latency-critical job that tracked failed login attempts for a few thousand admin accounts ran on the HashMapStateBackend, because the state was tiny and we wanted microsecond access to gate sensitive systems. A huge job that kept a rolling ninety-day transaction history per account across hundreds of millions of retail accounts for fraud scoring ran on the EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend, because that state was far too large for heap, grew continuously, and had to checkpoint efficiently. I could demonstrate the key difference concretely: when only a handful of accounts changed between checkpoints, the heap backend still paid a full snapshot of all state while RocksDB uploaded only the few changed entries incrementally. Being able to explain the heap-speed versus disk-scale tradeoff, and above all that incremental checkpointing is usually the deciding factor for many-gigabyte state, is exactly the kind of operational judgment that marks real Flink production experience.
